quiz.question: A HashMap lookup misses an object that was previously put with an equal key. What contract break is the most likely cause?
options: equals is reflexive but hashCode is never called for stored keys
equals is true for two keys whose hashCode values differ
hashCode is cached once at construction and never changes
compareTo is inconsistent with equals but hashCode is consistent
quiz.explanation: If a.equals(b) is true, a.hashCode() must equal b.hashCode(). HashMap buckets by hash first, so unequal hashes make equal keys unreachable.

quiz.question: You mutate a field that participates in hashCode after inserting the object into a HashSet. What happens on later contains()?
options: The set rehashes the object automatically on mutation
contains() still finds it because identity is used as a fallback
The object is typically lost: it sits in the old bucket while lookup uses the new hash
The set throws ConcurrentModificationException on the next read
quiz.explanation: Hash-based collections do not track field mutations. Changing a hash-relevant field after insert leaves the object in the wrong bucket.

quiz.question: Two objects are equal by business id but you include a mutable timestamp in hashCode only. Which failure appears first?
options: TreeMap ordering becomes unstable
equals remains consistent while hash buckets diverge after the timestamp changes
identityHashCode starts colliding
serialization identity is lost
quiz.explanation: equals and hashCode must use the same significant fields. A field in hashCode but not equals (or a field that changes after insert) breaks the map/set contract.

quiz.question: Why must hashCode be consistent with equals even when you never put the type in a HashMap yourself?
options: The compiler verifies the contract at compile time
Libraries, caches, distinct(), groupingBy, and framework identity maps rely on it
The JVM uses hashCode to decide GC generations
Thread interruption delivery keys off hashCode
quiz.explanation: Any hash-based structure in the JDK or a framework will mis-behave if the contract is broken, including streams and ORM snapshots.

quiz.question: An equals implementation returns true for a subclass instance with extra state. What is the usual hazard?
options: hashCode becomes slower
Symmetry or transitivity breaks when the subclass equals does not agree
The parent class can no longer be garbage collected
instanceof is illegal in equals
quiz.explanation: Allowing cross-type equality without a careful canEqual/getClass strategy commonly violates symmetry or transitivity.

quiz.question: getClass() vs instanceof in equals: which statement is accurate for value types used as map keys?
options: instanceof is always required so proxies can equal the real type
getClass() prevents a subclass with extra fields from equaling the parent, preserving transitivity
Both are equivalent if hashCode is final
instanceof is required by the language specification
quiz.explanation: getClass() equality rejects subclass instances, which is the conservative choice for types that will live in hash collections.

quiz.question: You implement equals on a JPA entity using a generated database id that is null before persist. What goes wrong in a HashSet of new entities?
options: All new entities collide as equal and collapse to one set element, or change bucket after persist
HashSet refuses null hash codes
Persist becomes a no-op
The persistence context ignores equals
quiz.explanation: Null ids make every transient entity equal (or all hash to the same bucket). After id assignment, hashCode changes and the set loses the entity.

quiz.question: A correct hashCode for a class with several fields should:
options: XOR System.identityHashCode of each field only
Combine the same fields equals uses, with a mixing function that spreads bits
Return a constant to maximize cache hits
Delegate to Object.hashCode to preserve identity
quiz.explanation: hashCode must be derived from the equality-significant state and should distribute well to keep buckets short.

quiz.question: Two equal objects must have equal hashCodes. The converse is:
options: Also required: unequal objects must have unequal hashCodes
Not required; collisions are legal and expected
Required only for Strings
Required only inside ConcurrentHashMap
quiz.explanation: Collisions are allowed. Only the one-way implication equals ⇒ same hashCode is mandatory.

quiz.question: Why is a constant hashCode (always 42) technically contract-legal but operationally disastrous?
options: It violates reflexivity of equals
Every key lands in one bucket, turning HashMap operations into linear scans
The JIT refuses to inline equals
It disables escape analysis
quiz.explanation: A constant hash satisfies the contract if equals is consistent, but destroys the O(1) assumption of hash collections.

quiz.question: When is it acceptable to not override hashCode?
options: Whenever equals is overridden with business fields
When you keep Object identity equality and never treat the type as a value key
When the class is Serializable
When the class is abstract
quiz.explanation: If equals is not overridden, identity equality and identity hash remain consistent. Overriding equals without hashCode is the bug.

quiz.question: A record's generated equals/hashCode vs a mutable class: which production rule still applies?
options: Records may omit hashCode because components are final
Do not mutate record-equivalent state after the instance is used as a hash key; records just make that state explicit
Records hash only the first component
Mutable classes cannot implement equals
quiz.explanation: Immutability makes the contract easy to keep. The underlying rule is still: hash-relevant state must be stable while the object is in a hash collection.

quiz.question: compareTo disagrees with equals for a class used in both HashSet and TreeSet. What do you observe?
options: Both sets always agree on membership
An object can be 'in' one set and 'not in' the other for the same logical value
TreeSet automatically delegates to hashCode
HashSet sorts using compareTo
quiz.explanation: Sorted collections use compareTo; hash collections use equals/hashCode. Inconsistency yields split-brain membership.

quiz.question: Floating-point fields in equals/hashCode are dangerous mainly because:
options: NaN is not equal to itself, so equals can break reflexivity
doubles cannot be hashed
The JVM forbids floating fields in equals
hashCode of 0.0 and -0.0 is unspecified and crashes
quiz.explanation: NaN != NaN under IEEE rules, so a naive ==/equals on a NaN field makes an object not equal to itself. Use compare/bit conversion with an explicit NaN policy.

flashcards.back: If a.equals(b) then a.hashCode() == b.hashCode(); hashCode may collide when equals is false. Both must use the same significant, stable fields.

flashcards.front: Why mutating a key after HashMap.put loses the entry
flashcards.back: The entry stays in the bucket of the old hash. Lookup computes a new hash and searches a different bucket, so get/contains miss.
getClass() rejects subclasses and protects transitivity for map keys. instanceof allows mixed-type equality and needs a canEqual pattern to stay safe.

flashcards.front: JPA entity equals on generated id
flashcards.back: Transient entities share null id and collapse or collide; after persist the id (and hash) changes and hash collections lose them. Prefer a stable business key or identity until assigned.
Returning a constant satisfies the contract and puts every key in one bucket, making HashMap/HashSet linear and contention-heavy.
Whenever you override equals. Skip both only if identity equality is the intended semantics.
HashSet membership and TreeSet membership can disagree for the same pair of objects, breaking uniqueness assumptions across APIs.
A field that is NaN makes a.equals(a) false if you use ==. That violates reflexivity and poisons every hash collection.

quiz.question: In a generational heap, promotion means:
options: Moving a live object from a young generation space into the old generation after surviving collections
Raising a thread's priority when it allocates
Compacting the metaspace into the nursery
Converting a stack allocation into a heap allocation
quiz.explanation: Objects that survive enough young collections (or do not fit in young) are promoted to old. Old collections are rarer and more expensive.

quiz.question: Premature promotion usually shows up as:
options: Lower allocation rate and smaller heaps
Old generation filling with short-lived objects, causing frequent expensive old/mixed/full collections
Stack overflow on deep recursion
Direct ByteBuffer leaks only
quiz.explanation: If the nursery is too small or survivor spaces overflow, objects that would have died young get tenured and force old-gen GC.

quiz.question: A sudden spike of promotions during a traffic burst is most often caused by:
options: Young generation / survivor spaces too small for the live set of the burst
Too many daemon threads
JIT disabling escape analysis permanently
Finalizers running on the main thread
quiz.explanation: When eden/survivors cannot hold the burst's still-live objects, the collector promotes them to make room.

quiz.question: Why can promoting many objects increase pause times even if the heap is not full?
options: Promotion always stops the world until the disk is fsynced
Old-gen collections, remembered-set scanning, and fragmentation/copy work grow with the tenured live set
The OS swaps the young generation first
Promotion disables biased locking
quiz.explanation: A larger old live set means more marking/copying/RS scanning. Fragmentation from promotions also forces compaction.

quiz.question: Allocation failure in eden that promotes a huge live set in one young GC is called:
options: A promotion storm / survivor overflow
A safepoint leak
A biased-lock revocation
A compressed-oops failure
quiz.explanation: If survivors cannot absorb live young objects, they are promoted en masse. Logs show high promotion rates and old-gen growth.

quiz.question: Caches that retain objects slightly longer than the young-gen lifetime cause:
options: No GC impact because caches are off-heap by default
Steady promotion of cache entries into old gen, then mixed/full GC when they expire later
Only metaspace collection
Thread-local allocation buffer disablement
quiz.explanation: TTL/size caches often keep data just long enough to tenure. Expiry then creates old-gen garbage — the worst of both worlds.

quiz.question: A large object that does not fit in young generation is typically:
options: Rejected with OutOfMemoryError immediately
Allocated directly in old generation (or a large-object space), skipping young survival
Split across eden and stack
Stored in metaspace
quiz.explanation: Humongous/large allocations bypass the nursery and tenure immediately, accelerating old-gen pressure.

quiz.question: Which application pattern most reliably increases promotion volume?
options: Short-lived per-request objects that die in eden
Building large intermediate graphs (JSON trees, ORM entities, byte[] buffers) that remain live across a young GC
Primitive local variables
Using stack-confined objects that never escape
quiz.explanation: Anything still reachable at the next young collection is a promotion candidate. Fat request graphs and buffers are classic.

quiz.question: Old generation fragmentation after repeated promotions of mixed-size objects leads to:
options: Faster young GCs
Promotion failures: young GC cannot tenure objects and escalates to a full/concurrent-mode failure collection
Automatic heap shrinkage
Disablement of TLABs only
quiz.explanation: If old gen has free bytes but not a contiguous region, promotion fails and the collector falls back to a heavier collection.

quiz.question: How do you confirm premature promotion from GC logs rather than guessing?
options: Watch only CPU steal time
Correlate high promotion bytes / shrinking survivor-to-old flow with rising old occupancy and mixed/full GC frequency
Count classloader counts
Measure only socket buffer sizes
quiz.explanation: Promotion rate, survivor overflow, and old occupancy together diagnose tenuring of short-lived objects.

quiz.question: Raising young generation size can reduce premature promotion because:
options: Objects get more time to die before a young collection copies them
Old generation is deleted
hashCode caching is enabled
Finalizers run twice
quiz.explanation: A larger nursery increases the chance that request-scoped objects become unreachable before they are tenured. It also makes each young pause bigger — a tradeoff.

quiz.question: Tenuring threshold too low means:
options: Objects must survive many young GCs before old gen, reducing promotion
Objects are promoted after few survivals, tenuring data that might still die soon
No object can enter old gen
Eden is never collected
quiz.explanation: Adaptive tenuring can drop the threshold under allocation pressure, which is exactly how bursts create premature promotion.

quiz.question: Why do long-lived static collections of request data cause old-gen GC pain?
options: Statics are stored in registers
They keep objects reachable until removed, so they promote and then sit as old garbage or live set forever
The JIT inlines them into young gen
They disable card marking
quiz.explanation: Reachability, not allocation site, decides lifetime. Unbounded static maps tenure everything they hold.

quiz.question: A service allocates huge short-lived byte[] for each request. Young GC is frequent and old gen still grows. Best first hypothesis?
options: The arrays are humongous/large and allocated in old/humongous space, or they survive because the request spans a young GC
byte[] is never collected
The compiler boxes each byte
Promotion only happens for objects with finalizers
quiz.explanation: Large arrays skip the nursery; medium arrays that remain live across a young pause get promoted. Both show as old-gen growth despite 'short-lived' intent.

flashcards.back: Copying a still-reachable object from young generation into old generation after it survives collections (or because it would not fit in young).
Short-lived objects tenure because eden/survivors are too small, the tenuring threshold is too low, or the object is too large. Result: old-gen GC churn.
Live young objects do not fit in survivor space, so the collector promotes them in bulk during a young GC.
TTL slightly longer than the young-gen lifetime keeps entries alive through a young GC. They promote, then become old garbage when the TTL expires.
Objects that do not fit in the nursery are allocated directly in old or a large-object space, so they never get a cheap death in eden.
Old generation has no contiguous room (often fragmentation). Young GC cannot tenure and the collector escalates to a full or concurrent-mode-failure collection.
High promotion bytes, survivor overflow, rapidly rising old occupancy, then mixed/full GCs — not just 'GC happened'.
Larger young gen lets request objects die before tenuring but makes each young pause copy more. Tune from promotion rate and pause budget, not folklore.

quiz.question: newFixedThreadPool(n) uses which queue, and why does that matter in an outage?
options: A bounded ArrayBlockingQueue that rejects when full
An unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue, so tasks accumulate in memory instead of rejecting
A SynchronousQueue that never buffers
The fork-join work-stealing queue only
quiz.explanation: Executors.newFixedThreadPool and newSingleThreadExecutor use an unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. Under overload the heap grows until GC thrash or OOM; callers are not failed fast.

quiz.question: With a core-sized pool and an unbounded queue, when are extra threads above corePoolSize created?
options: Whenever the queue has more than one task
Never, because the queue never appears 'full', so max threads are not started
Immediately on the first submit
Only after a keep-alive timeout
quiz.explanation: ThreadPoolExecutor creates threads beyond core only when the queue is full. An unbounded queue is never full, so maximumPoolSize is dead code.

quiz.question: The production failure mode of an unbounded executor queue is typically:
options: Immediate RejectedExecutionException that pages on-call
Latency explosion, heap growth, GC thrash, then OOM or instance death while work still looks 'accepted'
The pool shuts down automatically
The OS kills only the idle threads
quiz.explanation: Submit succeeds, so SLIs that watch error rate stay green while the queue hides hours of work and memory.

quiz.question: A bounded queue plus AbortPolicy is preferred under overload because:
options: It converts overload into a fast failure the caller can shed, retry, or trip a breaker on
It guarantees every task eventually runs
It disables GC
It raises thread priority
quiz.explanation: Backpressure must be visible. Rejection is a feature: it protects the JVM and signals upstream to stop sending.

quiz.question: CallerRunsPolicy on a saturated pool does what, and what is the hidden risk?
options: Drops the task silently; no risk
Runs the task on the submitting thread, which backpressures that thread — and can deadlock a request thread that also needs the pool
Starts unlimited extra threads
Persists tasks to disk
quiz.explanation: Caller-runs is useful for CPU pools fed by non-request threads. On servlet/event loops it can stall the only threads that drain other work.

quiz.question: Why does monitoring thread-pool activeCount==coreSize miss an unbounded-queue outage?
options: activeCount includes queued tasks
Workers are busy at core size while the queue length and heap are the actual overload signals
JMX cannot read executors
coreSize is always zero
quiz.explanation: The pool looks fully utilized and healthy. Queue depth, task wait time, and heap are the metrics that show the impending OOM.

quiz.question: A common HTTP-client antipattern: unbounded pool queue in front of a slow dependency. What happens to the inbound request threads?
options: They fail immediately with 503
They block on Future.get/callback lag while the executor queue absorbs more calls, exhausting the inbound pool too
They are migrated to the executor automatically
They skip the client timeout
quiz.explanation: Work is accepted faster than the dependency can serve it. Both the executor queue and the servlet/tomcat pool fill. Cascading saturation.

quiz.question: SynchronousQueue with a cached thread pool fails in the opposite way. What is that failure?
options: Tasks queue forever
Every extra task creates a thread (or rejects if a cap is hit); thread explosion or native memory death under burst
No task ever runs
The queue stores the entire heap
quiz.explanation: newCachedThreadPool uses SynchronousQueue and unbounded max threads. No buffering: bursts become threads, not heap, until the machine dies.

quiz.question: For a latency-sensitive request path, the safe default executor shape is:
options: Unbounded queue, fixed threads, no timeout
Bounded queue, explicit max threads, rejection handler, task timeout, and queue-depth metrics
Cached pool with no limit
A new thread per task
quiz.explanation: Bound memory and concurrency, fail fast, observe queue wait. That is the production contract.

quiz.question: Why can an unbounded queue make timeouts ineffective?
options: Timeouts cannot be set on Future
The timeout often starts only when the task begins running; queued wait is invisible until the worker dequeues it
LinkedBlockingQueue ignores interrupts
GC disables timers
quiz.explanation: A 200ms task timeout is useless if the task sat in the queue for 30s. Bound the queue and measure time-in-queue.

quiz.question: OOM with a heap full of Runnable/Callable wrappers and captured request state points to:
options: Metaspace leak from proxies
An unbounded executor (or unbounded instrumented queue) retaining submitted work
Stack overflow
Direct buffer leak only
quiz.explanation: Heap dumps of production outages from unbounded pools show millions of task objects, not just business entities.

quiz.question: You set maximumPoolSize=32 but still never see more than 8 threads. Likely cause?
options: The OS thread cap is 8
corePoolSize=8 and the work queue is unbounded, so the pool never saturates the queue
JIT inlines the workers
maximumPoolSize only applies to scheduled executors
quiz.explanation: This is the ThreadPoolExecutor trap. max is consulted only after offer() fails.

quiz.question: A scheduled executor with an unbounded delayed queue plus a slow task causes:
options: Tasks to skip automatically
Schedule pile-up: overlapping runs queue up, delay grows without bound, heap and lag explode
The scheduler switches to a bounded queue
Fixed rate becomes fixed delay automatically
quiz.explanation: If a job takes longer than its period, executions accumulate. Guard with a single-flight lock or skip-if-running, and bound the queue.

quiz.question: Which rejection story is honest to upstream load balancers?
options: Accept every task into RAM and die five minutes later
Reject at the executor or servlet container so the LB can shed to healthy instances immediately
Log and swallow RejectedExecutionException
Start a new JVM per rejected task
quiz.explanation: Failing the request lets the load balancer and client retry elsewhere. Silent queueing concentrates load on the already-sick instance.

flashcards.back: Unbounded LinkedBlockingQueue. Tasks are never rejected; they accumulate in heap. maximumPoolSize is effectively ignored.

flashcards.front: When ThreadPoolExecutor starts threads above core
flashcards.back: Only when workQueue.offer fails (queue full). Unbounded queues never fail offer, so extra threads never start.
Success rate stays high, latency and heap climb, GC thrashes, then OOM. Workers look 'busy but healthy' at core size.
Bounded queue, explicit max threads, Abort (or a carefully chosen) handler, timeouts that include queue wait, and metrics for queue depth and wait.
The submitting thread runs the task. On request threads this can deadlock or stall the inbound pool that was supposed to stay available.
SynchronousQueue + unbounded max threads: bursts create threads until native memory or context switching dies, instead of filling the heap.
Task timeouts usually start at run(), not submit(). Unbounded queues hide minutes of wait that no downstream timeout sees.

flashcards.front: Why reject is kinder than queue
flashcards.back: Rejection is visible backpressure. The load balancer can shift traffic. Silent queueing pins overload to one JVM until it crashes.

quiz.question: Happens-before is:
options: A wall-clock ordering of statements
A JMM guarantee that memory writes before a given action are visible to reads after a related action
The order the JIT must emit instructions on one core
A debugger stepping rule
quiz.explanation: If A happens-before B, then A's side effects are visible to B. It is about visibility and ordering, not measured time.

quiz.question: Two threads write and read a non-volatile field with no lock. What does the JMM allow?
options: The reader must see the latest write
The reader may see a stale value indefinitely; there is no happens-before
The JVM throws a visibility exception
The write is automatically flushed at end of the method
quiz.explanation: Without a synchronization action, compilers and CPUs may keep writes in registers/store buffers forever from another thread's perspective.

quiz.question: Which pair establishes happens-before?
options: Thread A writes x; thread B reads x later on the wall clock
Unlock of monitor M happens-before a subsequent lock of the same M
Two volatile writes to different fields in either order
Starting a thread happens-before every write in the parent after start
quiz.explanation: Unlock-lock on the same monitor is a standard HB edge. Wall-clock later is not HB. Thread.start HB only the started thread's first action, not later parent writes.

quiz.question: A volatile write happens-before a subsequent volatile read of the same variable. What else becomes visible?
options: Only that volatile field
All writes in the writing thread that happened-before that volatile write
All writes in the entire JVM
Only writes to final fields
quiz.explanation: Volatile is a synchronization action with a release/acquire flavor: it publishes prior writes in that thread, not the whole heap from other threads.

quiz.question: The classic 'check flag then read payload' bug is fixed by:
options: Making only the payload non-volatile
Making the flag volatile (or using a lock/atomic) so the payload writes that happened-before the flag write become visible
Adding more sleep() in the reader
Using a larger heap
quiz.explanation: The flag write must HB the flag read. Then transitivity makes earlier payload writes visible. Sleep is not a memory barrier.

quiz.question: final field safety guarantees what for constructors?
options: All fields of the object are visible after the constructor, including non-final
A properly constructed object's final fields are visible to any thread that sees the published reference, without extra sync
final fields can be written by other threads freely
escape of this in the constructor is always safe
quiz.explanation: Freeze at the end of the constructor publishes final fields. Leaking this during construction, or mutating finals via reflection/unsafe, voids the guarantee. Non-final fields still need publication.

quiz.question: Thread.start() happens-before the first action in the started thread. Thread termination happens-before:
options: Any later join() that successfully returns
Any later interrupt of a third thread
The next GC
Any write in the parent thread
quiz.explanation: join (and Thread.get/isAlive after termination, in effect via join) observes the worker's writes. Fire-and-forget threads do not publish back.

quiz.question: Why is synchronized (this) on a setter insufficient if a getter reads the field with no lock and no volatile?
options: synchronized never flushes writes
There is no happens-before to the getter, so it may see stale data
Getters cannot be inlined
this cannot be used as a monitor
quiz.explanation: HB for monitors requires both the write-side unlock and a later lock on the same monitor (or another sync edge). One-sided locking does not publish to unsynchronized readers.

quiz.question: Double-checked locking without volatile on the instance field is broken because:
options: synchronized cannot be used in constructors
A reader can see a non-null reference before the constructor writes are visible
hashCode of the singleton changes
The classloader deadlocks
quiz.explanation: Publishing the reference without a freeze/volatile/lock allows a racy reader to observe a partially constructed object.

quiz.question: Happens-before is transitive. That matters because:
options: You must declare transitivity in equals
A lock/volatile edge can carry an entire chain of earlier writes to a later reader
The GC uses transitivity to promote objects
It forces sequential consistency for all fields
quiz.explanation: Program order plus a single release/acquire pair can publish many preceding writes. That is why a volatile flag can publish a whole payload.

quiz.question: Which statement about data races is correct?
options: A data race is only a performance issue; values are still well-defined
A data race (conflicting accesses with no HB) makes behavior undefined for those accesses; you can see torn/stale/impossible values
The JMM forbids the JIT from reordering around a data race
AtomicInteger still has data races on get/set
quiz.explanation: Correct concurrent programs must be data-race-free. Atomics/volatiles/locks exist to eliminate the race, not to paper over it.

quiz.question: ConcurrentHashMap publication of an object as a value: after a successful put, another thread's get of that key:
options: May still see a stale object graph unless all fields are volatile
Happens-after the put, so writes that HB the put are visible to the getter of that entry
Requires an extra synchronized around every field read forever
Ignores happens-before because CHM is lock-free
quiz.explanation: ConcurrentHashMap (and blocking queues, etc.) define HB between a successful write and a later read of that mapping. The published object's fields written before put are visible.

quiz.question: volatile ++ (read-modify-write) is not atomic. How does that relate to happens-before?
options: HB and atomicity are the same thing
Each volatile read/write has HB/visibility, but increment is two accesses; two threads can still lose an update
volatile forbids lost updates by definition
The compiler turns volatile++ into a CAS
quiz.explanation: Visibility ≠ atomicity. Use AtomicInteger or a lock for counters. volatile is for publication and flags, not for compound actions.

quiz.question: A long/double field on a 64-bit JVM without volatile: is a torn read still possible, and is visibility guaranteed?
options: Atomicity of 64-bit writes is not the same as HB; without a sync edge, another thread may never see the write at all
long is always sequentially consistent
The JMM makes all 64-bit fields volatile
Torn reads are the only issue; visibility is automatic
quiz.explanation: Do not confuse word tearing with publication. Even if a write is atomic, without HB the reader can cache an old value forever.

flashcards.back: A JMM relation: if A HB B, then A's memory effects are visible to B and A is ordered before B. Wall-clock time is irrelevant.
A plain field write may never become visible to another thread. Compilers and CPUs are allowed to keep it in a register or store buffer.
Unlock of monitor M happens-before a later lock of the same M. Both sides must use the same lock; one-sided synchronized does not publish.
A volatile write HB a later volatile read of that variable, and carries all writes in that thread that HB the volatile write (release/acquire).
After a constructor finishes, final fields are visible to any thread that sees the published reference — unless this escaped during construction.
start() HB the first action of the new thread. Termination HB a successful join(), so the joiner sees the worker's writes.
The instance field must be volatile (or initialized via a holder class). Otherwise a reader can see a non-null, uninitialized object.
volatile/HB publish values. They do not make read-modify-write atomic. Counters and check-then-act still need atomics or locks.

quiz.question: Optional's intended use in application code is primarily:
options: A mutable field type on every domain entity
A return type that makes absence explicit at the call site
A replacement for null in method parameters
A serializable column type for JPA
quiz.explanation: Optional was designed as a return type. Using it as a field, parameter, or persistence mapping is usually a misuse with real costs.

quiz.question: Calling get() without isPresent() is a problem because:
options: get() is deprecated and always returns null
It throws NoSuchElementException — a louder null, not a safer API
It boxes the value twice
It returns a default empty string
quiz.explanation: Blind get() recreates NPE with a different name. Prefer orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, ifPresent, or map/flatMap.

quiz.question: orElse(computeExpensive()) vs orElseGet(this::computeExpensive): the production bug is:
options: orElseGet always runs the supplier
orElse evaluates its argument eagerly even when the Optional is present, wasting work or causing side effects
orElseGet cannot return null
They are identical at runtime
quiz.explanation: orElse's argument is always evaluated. Logging, RPC, and object creation in orElse(...) run on the happy path too.

quiz.question: Why is Optional as a field on a hot domain object a performance and null-safety lose?
options: Optional cannot be stored on the heap
You add an extra allocation and still can store a null Optional reference; nested emptiness is confusing
The JIT cannot inline methods that return Optional
Fields cannot be generic
quiz.explanation: A null Optional field is legal. You now have null and Optional.empty as two absences, plus boxing overhead in every instance.

quiz.question: Passing Optional as a method parameter is discouraged because:
options: The compiler rejects it
Callers wrap clumsily, overloads explode, and you still must handle a null Optional plus empty
Optional cannot be in bytecode
It breaks happens-before
quiz.explanation: Overload the method or use a clearer type. Parameters that are Optional invite optional.orElse(null) at every call site.

quiz.question: Optional.of(nullable) is wrong when the value may be null because:
options: of() accepts null and stores it
of() throws NullPointerException immediately; ofNullable is the API for unknown nullness
ofNullable throws on null
of() returns empty on null
quiz.explanation: of() is for known-non-null. ofNullable() maps null to empty. Mixing them is a common NPE source.

quiz.question: Returning Optional from a JPA repository method that can return many rows is a misuse because:
options: Optional cannot wrap entities
Non-unique results throw, and Optional pretends uniqueness that the query does not guarantee
Spring cannot proxy Optional
Optional disables transactions
quiz.explanation: Use List/Stream/Page. Optional means 0 or 1. Multiple rows are an error, not empty.

quiz.question: if (opt.isPresent()) { use(opt.get()); } is inferior to map/ifPresent mainly because:
options: It is slower in all cases
It is verbose, easy to call get() on the wrong Optional, and blocks fluent transformation of absence
isPresent is asynchronous
get() returns Optional again
quiz.explanation: The unwrap dance reintroduces the null-check style Optional was meant to replace. Chain map/flatMap/filter/orElse.

quiz.question: Optional in a Serializable DTO / Jackson field typically causes:
options: Automatic compact JSON
Awkward JSON (nested object or module-specific shape), extra null problems, and poor interop
Faster serialization than raw fields
Required presence of the field
quiz.explanation: Wire formats want nullable fields or absent properties, not a Java-only container. Map at the API boundary instead.

quiz.question: orElseThrow(MyException::new) vs orElseThrow(() -> new MyException(ctx)): choose based on:
options: Always prefer the constructor reference
Whether the exception needs captured context; the supplier is lazy and can close over useful state
orElseThrow cannot take a supplier
Exceptions must be preallocated
quiz.explanation: The supplier runs only on absence. Use it to build a message with ids and inputs; do not prebuild exceptions in orElseThrow(prebuilt).

quiz.question: Optional<Optional<T>> or Optional of a collection that may be empty usually means:
options: A recommended way to express two-level absence
Confused domain: flatten to Optional<T>, or return an empty collection, not both
Faster lookups
Required for stream flatMap
quiz.explanation: Empty list already means none. Optional<List> creates four states (null, empty optional, optional of null, optional of empty list) if mixed with nulls.

quiz.question: filter/map on Optional vs Stream: the trap is:
options: Optional.map does not unwrap nested Optionals; use flatMap when the function returns Optional
Optional.filter removes the Optional type
map is illegal on empty
flatMap is only for lists
quiz.explanation: map(f) where f returns Optional<U> yields Optional<Optional<U>>. That is the same nested-optional bug as in streams.

quiz.question: Using Optional to 'document' a Map.get is often worse than:
options: Leaving raw null and hoping
Optional.ofNullable(map.get(k)) at the edge, or a getOptional helper — not storing Optional values inside the map
Wrapping every value at insert time as Optional.ofNullable
Replacing Map with Hashtable
quiz.explanation: Maps already have null-value and missing-key ambiguity. Putting Optional in the map doubles the wrapper tax and still allows missing keys.

quiz.question: Which is a legitimate, production-grade Optional use?
options: public void setName(Optional<String> name)
public Optional<User> findUser(Id id) implemented with ofNullable, consumed via map/orElseThrow
class User { Optional<String> nickname; }
Optional as a JPA @Column type without a converter
quiz.explanation: Return-type Optional consumed functionally is the sweet spot. Parameters, fields, and persistence mappings are the usual misuses.

flashcards.back: A return type that forces the caller to confront absence. Not a field, not a parameter, not a persistence type, not a Map value wrapper.
of(null) throws NPE. ofNullable(null) is empty. Use of only when the value is known non-null.
orElse always evaluates its argument. orElseGet runs the supplier only on empty. Never put RPC, logging, or allocation in orElse(...).
Throws NoSuchElementException. It is not safer than NPE. Use orElse, orElseGet, orElseThrow, ifPresent, map.
Extra allocation per instance, and the field reference itself can be null — two absences. Store a nullable T (or a sentinel) instead.
map() on a function that returns Optional produces Optional<Optional<T>>. Use flatMap. Do not return Optional of an empty collection.
Wire and DB layers want nullable columns and properties. Convert to Optional at the service boundary if you want it, not on the entity/DTO itself.
Reverts to null-check style. Chain filter/map/flatMap and terminate with orElse/orElseThrow so absence has one path.

quiz.question: Collections.synchronizedMap vs ConcurrentHashMap under high read/write mix: the scalability difference is:
options: They use the same lock
synchronizedMap serializes all operations on one mutex; ConcurrentHashMap allows concurrent reads and finer-grained writes
ConcurrentHashMap is always slower
synchronizedMap never blocks
quiz.explanation: A single intrinsic lock makes synchronized wrappers a bottleneck. CHM is designed for concurrent access.

quiz.question: You wrap a HashMap with synchronizedMap and iterate it from another thread. What is required?
options: Nothing; the wrapper synchronizes iterators automatically for the whole traversal
You must manually synchronize on the map during iteration, or you race and can throw ConcurrentModificationException
Iterators are fail-safe and lock-free
Iteration is forbidden
quiz.explanation: Each method is synchronized, but a compound iterate-and-act is not atomic unless you hold the map's lock for the whole loop.

quiz.question: ConcurrentHashMap iterators are:
options: Fail-fast like HashMap
Weakly consistent: they reflect some but not necessarily all concurrent updates, and do not throw CME
A frozen snapshot of the map at creation
Blocking until all writers drain
quiz.explanation: Do not assume a stable snapshot. Size and iteration during writes are approximate.

quiz.question: Why is ConcurrentHashMap.compute/putIfAbsent preferred over get-then-put?
options: They are faster to type
Check-then-act on CHM is still a race; the atomic compound methods close it
get-then-put is atomic on CHM
putIfAbsent always overwrites
quiz.explanation: Concurrency of individual ops does not make your multi-step business operation atomic. Use compute, merge, putIfAbsent.

quiz.question: Hashtable and Vector in modern services are usually the wrong choice because:
options: They are not thread-safe
Every method locks the whole collection, they are obsolete APIs, and they still do not make compound actions safe
They allow nulls like CHM
They are slower than ArrayList even on one thread only because of boxing
quiz.explanation: Coarse locks plus 1990s APIs. Prefer CHM, CopyOnWrite, or a dedicated lock around a plain HashMap when the protocol is richer.

quiz.question: CopyOnWriteArrayList is a good fit when:
options: Writes are frequent and reads rare
Reads dominate and the list is small; iterators see a stable snapshot, writes copy the array
You need O(1) random writes
You need null-hostile semantics like CHM
quiz.explanation: Listener lists and config snapshots fit. Using it as a general mutable list under write load allocates and copies constantly.

quiz.question: CHM does not allow null keys or values. synchronizedMap(HashMap) does. The production hazard is:
options: There is no hazard
A null value cannot distinguish 'missing' from 'present but null', and migrating to CHM will NPE
CHM stores null as Optional
synchronizedMap rejects nulls at runtime always
quiz.explanation: Null values in synchronized maps hide presence. CHM's NPE on null is a feature that forces an explicit Optional/sentinel.

quiz.question: A ConcurrentHashMap of request-scoped data that is never removed causes:
options: Automatic eviction
A bounded leak of keys/values, promotion into old gen, and eventual heap exhaustion — concurrency does not imply boundedness
The map to switch to weak keys
Thread interruption
quiz.explanation: Thread-safety ≠ lifecycle. Unbounded concurrent maps are a top production leak pattern.

quiz.question: When is a single-threaded HashMap behind a lock better than CHM?
options: Never
When you must atomically update several structures, or iterate a consistent view under the same lock as writes
When you need the highest read scaling
When keys are ints
quiz.explanation: CHM atomicity is per-key. Multi-map invariants need your own lock (or a concurrent component designed for the invariant).

quiz.question: synchronizedList(ArrayList) and index-based get/set from many threads: still broken because:
options: ArrayList cannot store objects
size-then-get is not atomic; an index can vanish between calls even though each call is synchronized
synchronizedList does not wrap get
Indexes start at 1
quiz.explanation: Compound sequences need an external synchronized (list) { ... } covering the whole protocol, or a concurrent structure with atomic operations.

quiz.question: ConcurrentLinkedQueue vs BlockingQueue for a worker pool:
options: They are interchangeable
CLQ is non-blocking and has no take() that waits; a worker pool usually wants a BlockingQueue for idle wait and backpressure
CLQ blocks producers when full
BlockingQueue cannot be bounded
quiz.explanation: Pick the collection for the protocol: park/wait, bounding, and draining, not just 'concurrent' in the class name.

quiz.question: size() on ConcurrentHashMap is:
options: A lock-free exact count at all times
O(n)-ish / weakly consistent; do not use it for admission control on a hot path as if it were a mutex-protected counter
Always zero
Forbidden
quiz.explanation: Treat CHM size as an estimate. If you need exact occupancy for a bound, use a semaphore or LongAdder you control.

quiz.question: Collections.synchronizedMap is sometimes acceptable when:
options: You need maximum multi-core scaling
Contention is low, the map is small, and you document the mutex (the map itself) for compound operations
You iterate without locking
You store nulls as CHM would
quiz.explanation: Low-contention correctness with a simple lock can be clearer than CHM plus racy check-then-act. High contention is the wrong place for it.

quiz.question: Which statement is true about ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent?
options: The mapping function may safely modify the same map for other keys without risk
The function must be side-effect-light and must not try to update the same map in ways that deadlock or recurse; it runs under per-key synchronization
It is identical to get-then-put
It allows null results to store null values
quiz.explanation: compute* methods hold a key's bin lock. Re-entering the map, blocking, or returning null (which stores nothing) are common production bugs.

flashcards.back: synchronizedMap/List lock the entire collection per call. ConcurrentHashMap allows concurrent reads and striped writes. Wrappers do not make iteration atomic.
Manually synchronize on the map for the whole iteration. Otherwise you race writers and can get ConcurrentModificationException.
Weakly consistent, no CME. Not a snapshot. size() is an estimate, not a lock-protected exact count.
Thread-safe collections still race on compound actions. Use putIfAbsent, compute, merge, or an external lock around the invariant.
Snapshot iterators, expensive writes (full array copy). Fits rare writes and many unsynchronized readers, e.g. listener lists.
CHM forbids null keys and values. synchronized HashMap allows them, which confuses missing vs null and breaks a later CHM migration.
A ConcurrentHashMap that only puts will still OOM. Concurrency does not provide eviction, backpressure, or multi-structure atomicity.
Mapping function runs under per-key lock. Do not block, do not re-enter the map unsafely, and do not expect a null return to insert a null value.

quiz.question: Spring's @Transactional on a public method is implemented by:
options: The compiler rewriting the method body
A proxy (JDK or CGLIB) that starts/commits/rolls back around calls that go through the proxy
The JVM verifying every bytecode invoke
AspectJ load-time weaving in every default Boot app
quiz.explanation: Default is Spring AOP proxies. Only external calls through the bean proxy hit the advisor. This is the root of self-invocation bugs.

quiz.question: this.otherTransactionalMethod() inside the same class typically:
options: Still starts a new transaction as annotated
Bypasses the proxy, so @Transactional on the callee is ignored
Always throws IllegalTransactionStateException
Forces a suspend of the outer transaction
quiz.explanation: Self-invocation is a direct Java call. No proxy, no interceptor, no transaction boundary (and no other AOP advice either).

quiz.question: A service method without @Transactional calls this.save() which is @Transactional. The save runs:
options: In a transaction started by save's annotation
With no transactional interceptor, so each repository call may auto-commit or join nothing as if save were a plain method
In a nested transaction always
Only if the class is final
quiz.explanation: The annotation on save never runs. You get whatever the repository's default is, not the service-level unit of work you thought you declared.

quiz.question: REQUIRED on caller, REQUIRES_NEW on callee, called via this.callee():
options: The inner method still suspends and starts a new transaction
REQUIRES_NEW is skipped; there is no inner boundary at all
Both annotations merge into NESTED
The outer transaction commits twice
quiz.explanation: Without the proxy, propagation on the inner method does not exist. This silently destroys the 'log in a separate tx' pattern.

quiz.question: Which visibility is ignored by the default proxy-based @Transactional?
options: public methods called through the proxy
private/package/protected methods: the annotation is typically not applied (CGLIB may subclass, but Spring's tx advisor does not advise non-public by default)
only static methods
only constructors
quiz.explanation: Annotating private methods is a no-op with Spring AOP. People 'fix' self-invocation by making the method private — that makes it worse.

quiz.question: A reliable fix for self-invocation when you must call another transactional method:
options: Add Thread.sleep so the proxy catches up
Move the method to another bean and inject it, or self-inject the proxy, or use AopContext.currentProxy() with expose-proxy, or switch to AspectJ weaving
Mark the class final
Use @Transactional on the field
quiz.explanation: The call must enter the proxy (or a real AspectJ-woven body). Splitting beans is the cleanest production fix.

quiz.question: Self-injection of the same service works because:
options: Spring injects the raw target
Spring injects the transactional proxy, so self.foo() is an advised call
It enables AspectJ compile-time weaving
It disables CGLIB
quiz.explanation: You must call through the injected reference, not this. Circular creation is the cost; constructor injection of self is trickier than setter/lazy.

quiz.question: Checked exceptions inside @Transactional by default:
options: Always roll back
Do not roll back unless rollbackFor includes them; RuntimeException and Error do
Commit twice
Disable the proxy
quiz.explanation: A self-invocation bug plus a checked exception is a double miss: no interceptor, and even with an interceptor, checked exceptions commit unless declared.

quiz.question: readOnly=true on a class-level @Transactional, then a self-called inner write method with readOnly=false:
options: The write method still participates in the outer read-only transaction if called via this, and the write may fail or silently do nothing useful
readOnly is ignored always
Spring starts a write tx automatically on flush
The inner annotation wins without a proxy
quiz.explanation: Without a new proxy call, there is no new attribute application. You stay in the outer read-only unit of work.

quiz.question: Why tests that call the method via the injected bean pass, but a production path that goes through this.method fails?
options: Tests disable AOP
The test invokes the proxy; the production code path is an internal call that skips interceptors
H2 does not support transactions
@Transactional is test-only
quiz.explanation: This is why 'it works in the controller test' and still corrupts data when a facade method fans out to this.save().

quiz.question: @Transactional on a non-Spring-managed object (new Service()) means:
options: Annotations are still discovered via the call stack
No proxy exists, so the annotation never applies
Spring weaves all new calls
The transaction starts at the first JDBC call anyway
quiz.explanation: Same family as self-invocation: no Spring proxy, no transaction interceptor. Always obtain collaborative beans from the context.

quiz.question: TransactionSynchronization afterCommit registered in a self-called method with ignored @Transactional will:
options: Always run after the repository commit you expected
Bind to whatever transaction is actually active (maybe none), so it may run immediately, never, or on the wrong unit of work
Create a new transaction to hang the sync on
Throw if no proxy
quiz.explanation: Synchronizations attach to the current ThreadLocal transaction. If the inner @Transactional did not start, your afterCommit is not the boundary you annotated.

quiz.question: CGLIB subclass proxies still fail self-invocation because:
options: CGLIB cannot subclass
this inside the target is the target instance, not the subclass proxy wrapper sitting in the bean factory
CGLIB copies annotations onto this
JDK proxies would work for self-calls
quiz.explanation: Both JDK and CGLIB proxies wrap the target. Internal this is the target. JDK proxies would not even apply to self calls on the concrete class.

quiz.question: The safest team rule to prevent this outage class is:
options: Put @Transactional on every private helper
Transactional methods are entry points on a dedicated component; they are never called with this from the same class
Disable proxies and use ThreadLocal Connection only
Prefer checked exceptions for rollback
quiz.explanation: Architecture: a transactional application service is invoked from the outside. Helpers that need a different propagation live on another bean.

flashcards.back: Spring applies transactions via a proxy. this.foo() is a direct call on the target, so the interceptor never runs.
The inner propagation is ignored. No suspend, no new transaction — the 'audit in a separate tx' pattern silently fails.
Default Spring AOP does not advise private/package/protected methods. The annotation is a comment.
Split into another bean, inject the proxy (self-inject / AopContext with exposeProxy), or use AspectJ weaving so the call is advised in-body.
Annotations do nothing on objects you construct yourself. No proxy, no transaction, no security, no retry.
RuntimeException and Error roll back. Checked exceptions commit unless rollbackFor is set — independent of, and compounding, the self-call bug.

flashcards.front: readOnly outer + write inner via this
flashcards.back: You remain in the outer read-only transaction. The inner readOnly=false never applies.
Transactional methods are public entry points on a boundary component. Different propagation means a different bean, not a private helper.

quiz.question: Open Session/EntityManager in View in Spring Boot means:
options: The persistence context is closed before the controller returns
The EntityManager/session stays open for the whole web request so the view can lazy-load
Only native SQL is allowed in templates
Transactions are disabled for GET
quiz.explanation: OSIV binds an EntityManager to the request thread and closes it after the view renders. Lazy associations can load during JSON serialization.

quiz.question: The N+1 problem under OSIV typically appears as:
options: One join query and no extras
One query for a collection of roots, then one query per root (or per association) while Jackson/Thymeleaf touches lazy fields
A single batch always
Only at startup
quiz.explanation: The service returned entities with unfetched associations. The view walking getters issues a query per object after the service transaction ended — but the session is still open.

quiz.question: Why OSIV hides LazyInitializationException and makes N+1 worse in production:
options: It closes the session earlier
Serialization succeeds slowly with hidden per-entity SQL instead of failing fast in the service layer
It batches all lazy loads by default
It disables Hibernate statistics
quiz.explanation: Without OSIV, the view would throw. With OSIV, you ship a correct-looking JSON payload that took 1+N round trips on the request thread.

quiz.question: OSIV holds a database connection (or at least a persistence context) across:
options: Only the @Transactional method
Template rendering / JSON serialization, which may include remote calls if you are sloppy — stretching pool occupancy
Application startup only
Scheduled tasks only
quiz.explanation: A long-open persistence context plus view work is how OSIV contributes to connection pool exhaustion, not only N+1.

quiz.question: The correct place to fetch associations needed by a response is:
options: In the Jackson getter via lazy load
In the repository/service query (join fetch, entity graph, or explicit query) inside the transactional boundary
In a @PreDestroy hook
In the OSIV filter after commit
quiz.explanation: The service should return a fully initialized graph or a DTO. The view should not be a query engine.

quiz.question: join fetch in a Collection-valued association without care can:
options: Never affect row counts
Multiply root rows (cartesian product), so you need distinct or a two-query pattern
Disable OSIV
Automatically paginate
quiz.explanation: Fetching multiple bags/lists in one join fetch is a classic Hibernate trap. Pagination + join fetch is especially wrong.

quiz.question: Disabling OSIV without fixing fetch plans results in:
options: Faster pages always
LazyInitializationException during serialization — the failures OSIV was papering over
No SQL at all
Automatic DTO mapping
quiz.explanation: Turn OSIV off in a test environment first; the exceptions tell you which graphs are incomplete.

quiz.question: Why DTO/projection queries defeat OSIV N+1 more cleanly than initializing proxies:
options: DTOs cannot be serialized
There is no lazy graph to walk; the query selected exactly the response fields
Projections keep the session open longer
Entities cannot be mapped to JSON
quiz.explanation: If the view never sees an entity proxy, it cannot trigger hidden SQL. That is the architectural fix.

quiz.question: batch fetching (default_batch_fetch_size) vs eliminating N+1:
options: Batching removes the extra queries entirely
It groups lazy loads into IN-queries (N/batch + 1), a mitigation, not a substitute for fetching what you need up front
It only works with OSIV off
It disables lazy loading
quiz.explanation: Batch size turns 1000 queries into 20. Still chatty, still tied to the view walking associations.

quiz.question: A JSON serializer calling getOrders() on each Customer during a list endpoint is dangerous because:
options: getters cannot run SQL
Each getter is a lazy load after the service thought the unit of work was done; list size multiplies round trips
Jackson ignores getters
OSIV blocks getters
quiz.explanation: Entity-as-API is the N+1 generator. Map to a response type with the collections you actually want.

quiz.question: Transactional service ends, OSIV still open: writes in the view layer can:
options: Never happen because the context is read-only
Dirty-flush unexpectedly if something mutates a managed entity during rendering (rare but nasty), or at least keep connections busy
Always roll back
Open a second OSIV
quiz.explanation: OSIV's persistence context may still be open and flushing according to flush mode. Views should be side-effect free.

quiz.question: Pagination plus OSIV lazy collections in the page content leads to:
options: Constant query count
Page size N extra queries (or worse with nested collections), destroying the point of pagination
Hibernate ignoring page size
OSIV closing per page row
quiz.explanation: A 'cheap' page of 20 entities can become 20+ collection queries during serialization. Measure SQL count per endpoint, not just service logs.

quiz.question: The production metric that catches OSIV N+1 is:
options: HTTP 200 rate only
SQL count / time per request correlated with collection size, plus connection hold time
Heap usage only
Bean creation time
quiz.explanation: If query count scales with result size, you have N+1. OSIV makes it show up in request latency rather than as an exception.

quiz.question: Best default for a JSON API application:
options: Leave OSIV on so Jackson can lazy-load freely
Disable OSIV, fetch or project in the service, return DTOs, fail on accidental lazy access
Use EAGER on every association
Open a new EntityManager per getter
quiz.explanation: EAGER globally is the other N+1 (or cartesian) disaster. Explicit fetch per use case plus OSIV off is the production stance for APIs.

flashcards.back: Spring Boot keeps the EntityManager bound to the web request until after view rendering, so lazy loads during JSON/HTML succeed.
Serialization would have thrown LazyInitializationException. OSIV lets each getter hit the database instead, turning a bug into silent query storms.
1 query for roots + 1 query per entity per touched association. List endpoints multiply this by page size.
Inside the transactional service/repository with join fetch, entity graphs, or DTO/projection queries — not in the serializer.
The persistence context (and often a connection) stays open through rendering. Slow views hold pool slots and amplify saturation.
Exposes LazyInitializationException at the true missing-fetch sites. Fix those with explicit fetches/DTOs, do not turn OSIV back on to silence them.
Collection join fetch duplicates roots and fights pagination. Prefer two queries or a graph designed for the use case; DISTINCT is not always enough.
Mitigates N+1 by IN-clause grouping. It does not make the view a legitimate place to load a graph.

quiz.question: The default Spring bean scope is:
options: prototype
singleton — one shared instance per container
request
thread
quiz.explanation: Unless you say otherwise, every injection of that type is the same instance. State on that instance is shared across requests/threads.

quiz.question: A singleton bean with mutable instance fields used per request is dangerous because:
options: Spring clones it per thread automatically
Concurrent requests race on the same fields; you get cross-request data leaks and corruption
Singletons cannot be injected
The GC cannot collect them
quiz.explanation: This is a classic user-id leak: a field set in one request is read in another. Keep singletons stateless; put request state in parameters or request-scoped beans.

quiz.question: Injecting a prototype into a singleton does what by default?
options: A new prototype is created on every method call
The singleton receives one prototype instance at injection time and reuses it forever
Spring rejects the injection
The prototype becomes request-scoped
quiz.explanation: Injection is a one-time wiring. Use Provider/ObjectFactory/Lookup or a scoped proxy if you need a new instance per use.

quiz.question: request scope in a singleton without a proxy fails because:
options: Request scope does not exist
The singleton is created at startup, outside a request; there is no request instance to inject unless a scoped proxy defers access
HTTP is not thread-safe
Controllers cannot be singletons
quiz.explanation: BeanCreationException at startup is the usual symptom. Scoped proxies (or ObjectProvider) resolve the instance on each call from the current request.

quiz.question: prototype beans' destruction callbacks:
options: Are always invoked by the container like singletons
Are not fully managed; the client that created/obtained the instance is responsible for cleanup
Run after every HTTP request automatically
Are illegal
quiz.explanation: Leaking prototypes that hold connections/threads is easy because Spring will not @PreDestroy them for you on arbitrary create calls.

quiz.question: Which is the right scope for a JPA EntityManager injected into a singleton service?
options: A shared singleton EntityManager field used by all threads
A thread-bound persistence context via @PersistenceContext (proxy), not a singleton EM you created once
prototype EntityManager stored on the service
application scope EM
quiz.explanation: EntityManagers are not thread-safe. The injected EM is a proxy that delegates to the current transactional/thread-bound context.

quiz.question: session-scoped beans in a REST API cluster are a hazard because:
options: They are always faster
HTTP session state is per node (unless replicated/sticky), so users bounce and lose or split state; it also pins memory
Session scope cannot store objects
Spring forbids session scope
quiz.explanation: Prefer stateless JWT/server resources. Session-scoped Spring beans couple you to sticky sessions and serialization issues.

quiz.question: A @Scope("thread") or custom thread scope without cleanup across thread-pool reuse causes:
options: No issue because threads are never reused
State leaking between unrelated tasks that share a pooled thread
The pool to create a new JVM
Scope to upgrade to request
quiz.explanation: Thread-locals and thread-scoped beans on executors must be cleared. Tomcat/request threads are pooled too.

quiz.question: Why are Spring MVC controllers singletons by default?
options: They cannot be request-scoped
Stateless handlers scale; making controllers prototype/request-scoped is usually hiding mutable fields that should not exist
The dispatcher cannot find prototypes
HTTP requires one controller per connection
quiz.explanation: If you needed request scope on a controller, you probably wanted a request DTO parameter instead of fields.

quiz.question: scoped proxy mode TARGET_CLASS vs INTERFACES:
options: Irrelevant
CGLIB vs JDK proxy for the lazy scoped target; concrete classes without interfaces need class proxy, and self-invocation issues still apply
TARGET_CLASS creates a new singleton
INTERFACES disable the scope
quiz.explanation: The proxy is what the singleton holds. Each method call on the proxy fetches the scoped target. Internal this calls on the target still skip the proxy.

quiz.question: Refreshing a @RefreshScope bean vs singleton collaborators that captured it at startup:
options: All field-injected references see new values automatically if they stored the target
Collaborators that injected the raw target keep the old instance; they need the refresh proxy, @ConfigurationProperties rebinding, or to read through the proxy each time
RefreshScope restarts the JVM
Singletons cannot inject RefreshScope beans
quiz.explanation: Same injection-time capture problem as prototype-in-singleton. Capture the proxy, not a copied primitive field at @PostConstruct.

quiz.question: prototype-scoped @Transactional bean obtained once and reused:
options: Gets a new transaction interceptor each call from the factory
Is one object; reuse is your problem, and it is a poor way to get transactions
Cannot have @Transactional
Automatically request-scopes the tx
quiz.explanation: Do not use prototype as a transaction boundary hack. Use a singleton service with method-level @Transactional called through the proxy.

quiz.question: Which state belongs on a singleton bean?
options: The current user's id
Thread-safe collaborators (clients, repos) and immutable config; no per-request mutable fields
The ServletRequest stored in a field
A non-thread-safe ArrayList of 'current items'
quiz.explanation: If a field would be wrong under concurrent requests, it does not belong on a singleton.

quiz.question: ObjectProvider<T> / Provider<T> for a prototype is used to:
options: Cache the first instance only
Ask the container for a new (or scoped) instance at the call site instead of capturing injection-time identity
Disable the bean
Make T a singleton
quiz.explanation: getObject() is the lookup. That is how a singleton legitimately uses prototypes or request-scoped beans without a scoped proxy.

flashcards.back: Singleton: one instance per Spring container, shared across threads and requests. Mutable fields are shared mutable state.
Cross-request leaks and races. Keep singletons stateless; pass request data as method arguments or true request-scoped beans.
Only one prototype is created at wiring time. Use ObjectProvider, @Lookup, or a scoped proxy for per-call instances.
Cannot inject a request-scoped target into a singleton at context refresh unless a scoped proxy defers lookup until a request exists.
Spring does not manage the full lifecycle of prototypes it hands out. If it holds resources, you close them.
Never share a raw EM as a singleton field. @PersistenceContext injects a proxy to the thread-bound persistence context.
Ties you to HTTP session stickiness/replication and memory. Prefer stateless services.
Lookup API so a singleton can obtain the current scoped/prototype instance on each use instead of capturing it once.

quiz.question: Connection pool exhaustion looks like:
options: Instant OOM without waiting
Threads blocked waiting for a connection until timeout, then errors; throughput collapses while CPU may look idle
The database rejecting authentication only
GC promotion storms only
quiz.explanation: Callers pile up on pool checkout. You see thread dumps stuck in getConnection, rising latency, then timeout exceptions.

quiz.question: Holding a connection while calling a remote HTTP API inside @Transactional causes exhaustion because:
options: HTTP uses the same TCP port as JDBC
The connection stays checked out for the whole transaction, including slow IO that does not need the database
Pools cannot coexist with HTTP
@Transactional closes the pool
quiz.explanation: Short transactions: do DB work, commit, then call out. Nested remote IO is the classic pool-starve pattern.

quiz.question: OSIV plus a slow JSON serialization or template:
options: Releases the connection at service return always
Can keep the persistence context and connection occupied until the response is written
Never uses the pool
Uses a second unbounded pool
quiz.explanation: View-layer lazy loads and a still-open session extend checkout time beyond the service method.

quiz.question: Pool size 10, Tomcat threads 200, each request needing a connection:
options: Spring will auto-expand the pool to 200
190 threads can block on the pool; you must size pool, timeouts, and inbound concurrency together
Extra threads share connections safely
The database serializes them without wait
quiz.explanation: Inbound concurrency × connection hold time = required pool. If the product exceeds pool size, you queue or die.

quiz.question: A leak of connections (checkout without close) happens when:
options: You always use try-with-resources / Spring-managed DataSourceUtils
Manual getConnection without close, or a transaction that never completes (stuck thread, missing commit, swallowed rollback)
Hikari is enabled
You use @Transactional on every public method including health checks only
quiz.explanation: Leak detection in the pooler reports stacks of unclosed checkouts. Hung transactions are as bad as forgotten close().

quiz.question: Lock wait in the database plus a small pool creates a deadlock of the application because:
options: Locks are held on checked-out connections; other requests need those connections to run the statements that would release the locks
The pool ignores the database
Spring upgrades isolation automatically
TCP keepalive drops locks
quiz.explanation: Convoy: lock holders occupy pool slots; waiters occupy the rest waiting for slots or locks. Timeouts must be shorter than cascade death.

quiz.question: Why connectionTimeout (checkout wait) must be finite and smaller than the HTTP timeout:
options: So the load balancer / caller fails fast instead of tying up all servlet threads behind an infinite pool wait
The database requires it for correctness of SQL
Infinite wait uses less memory
Hikari forbids finite timeouts
quiz.explanation: Infinite checkout wait turns a DB hiccup into a full inbound-thread deadlock. Fail, shed load, recover.

quiz.question: Multiple DataSources each with a large pool on one JVM:
options: Is always correct
Can exhaust database max_connections across instances: pool size × processes × DataSources must stay under the DB cap
Spring shares one physical connection
Idle connections do not count against the database
quiz.explanation: Idle pooled connections still occupy server slots. Over-sizing pools is a cluster-wide outage waiting for a traffic spike.

quiz.question: self-invocation skipped @Transactional that leaves autocommit queries vs a long outer transaction: exhaustion angle is:
options: No difference
An unexpectedly long outer transaction (or, conversely, extra checkouts from unbatched autocommit) both increase occupancy; know which connection you hold
Autocommit never uses the pool
Transactions do not check out connections
quiz.explanation: Hold time and checkout count are the two occupancy knobs. Transaction boundaries decide both.

quiz.question: A streaming query / open ResultSet inside a transaction:
options: Frees the connection immediately
Pins a connection for the entire stream consumption; slow consumers starve the pool
Moves the cursor off-heap without a connection
Is executed by the web client
quiz.explanation: Do not stream a ResultSet out to a slow HTTP client on the same connection you need for the rest of the app.

quiz.question: Thread pool unbounded queue + each task needs a DB connection:
options: The executor bounds the pool for you
Accepted tasks wait on the executor, then wait on the connection pool — memory and thread/pool saturation stacked
Tasks skip the DB if the pool is busy
Hikari starts a thread per connection automatically matching the executor
quiz.explanation: Two queues, no backpressure. Bound both and reject at the edge.

quiz.question: The first metrics to chart for this failure:
options: Only CPU
Active/idle/pending connections, checkout time, connection leak count, in-flight transactions, servlet thread occupancy
Only heap
Bean count
quiz.explanation: Pending threads > 0 and active == max for a sustained period is the smoking gun.

quiz.question: read-only health checks sharing the primary pool can exhaust it during an incident because:
options: Health checks do not use SQL
Probes compete with business traffic for the last connections, causing a death spiral of failed checks and restarts
Kubernetes ignores JDBC
read-only queries skip the pool
quiz.explanation: Isolate a tiny reserved pool or a cheap non-DB probe. Do not let liveness compete with checkout waiters.

quiz.question: Best structural fix for 'pool exhausted under load' when SQL is already fast:
options: Set pool size to 10,000
Shorten hold time: no remote calls in tx, no OSIV lazy I/O, bound inbound concurrency to roughly pool size × (1/hold-time), fail fast on checkout
Disable timeouts
Switch every query to EAGER join fetch without measuring
quiz.explanation: Pool size is a last-resort multiplier. Occupancy = arrivals × hold time. Cut hold time and arrivals first.

flashcards.back: Threads blocked in connection checkout, idle CPU, latency spike, then timeout. Not necessarily high DB CPU.

flashcards.front: Don't do IO in a transaction
flashcards.back: HTTP, queues, and sleep hold a checked-out connection. Do database work, commit, then call the world.
Needed connections ≈ concurrent requests that need the DB × hold time. Inbound threads should not wildly exceed what the pool and DB can serve.
Must be finite and shorter than the client/HTTP timeout so you fail fast instead of deadlocking the servlet pool.
instances × DataSources × maxPoolSize must stay under the database's max_connections, including idle sockets.
Unclosed connections and never-ending transactions permanently shrink the pool. Slow but closed transactions temporarily shrink it. Both page the same.
An open persistence context or ResultSet pins a connection through view rendering or stream consumption.
Do not let probes consume the last business connections. Reserve capacity or use a cheap check so incidents do not restart healthy-but-busy nodes.

quiz.question: Without a custom Executor bean, @Async often runs on:
options: The request thread (so it is not async)
A SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor that creates a new thread per task and does not reuse a bounded pool
The fork-join common pool only
The Tomcat worker that called it, always
quiz.explanation: Default async support is not a production thread pool. You can thread-explode or lose control of concurrency. Declare a bounded TaskExecutor.

quiz.question: @Async on a self-called method in the same class:
options: Still hops threads
Is ignored like other Spring AOP: the method runs synchronously on the caller thread
Always uses the default executor
Throws unless the class is final
quiz.explanation: Same proxy rule as @Transactional. Internal calls are not async.

quiz.question: An @Async method with an unbounded queue under a traffic spike:
options: Rejects immediately
Accepts work until heap/OOM while the caller thinks the job was safely offloaded
Runs inline on Tomcat threads automatically
Drops oldest tasks
quiz.explanation: This is the executor unbounded-queue outage, now triggered by a one-line annotation. Bound the queue and define a rejection policy.

quiz.question: Why request-thread ThreadLocals (security context, MDC, tenant) vanish in @Async:
options: ThreadLocals are copied by the JVM automatically
A new worker thread does not inherit them unless a TaskDecorator/propagating executor copies them
@Async is not allowed to log
SecurityContext is a singleton
quiz.explanation: You will log without request ids, and run without the authenticated user, unless you decorate the executor.

quiz.question: Exceptions from @Async void methods:
options: Propagate to the HTTP client
Go to the configured AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler; if you did not set one, they can be swallowed after a log
Retry forever
Roll back the caller's transaction automatically always
quiz.explanation: Fire-and-forget failures are silent unless you handle them. Prefer returning Future/CompletableFuture and observe completion.

quiz.question: @Async + @Transactional on the same method:
options: The transaction definitely runs on the caller and the work on the worker
Interceptor order matters; the transaction typically starts on the async thread after the hop — the caller's transaction does not cover the async body
They are illegal together
The caller always joins the async transaction
quiz.explanation: Do not expect the HTTP request's transaction to include async work. If you need after-commit async, use TransactionSynchronization afterCommit to submit.

quiz.question: Submitting @Async work before the caller transaction commits, and the async thread reading that row, causes:
options: A guaranteed read of committed data
A race: the worker may not see uncommitted data (or may block on locks), so jobs flake
Repeatable read across threads by default
The async thread to join the same JDBC connection
quiz.explanation: afterCommit scheduling is the correct pattern for 'do this once the row exists'.

quiz.question: A custom ThreadPoolTaskExecutor for @Async should be exposed by:
options: Replacing TaskExecutor with an unbounded cached pool to be safe
Implementing AsyncConfigurer / naming the executor in @Async("name") with bounded queue, size, and decorator
Using Executors.newFixedThreadPool without Spring lifecycle
Starting threads in @PostConstruct manually only
quiz.explanation: You want lifecycle (graceful shutdown), metrics, and the annotation to address a specific pool. Multiple pools beat one mixed workload pool.

quiz.question: Graceful shutdown of the @Async pool on SIGTERM:
options: Happens for SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor always
Requires a Spring-managed executor with waitForTasksToComplete / timeout; otherwise in-flight emails/jobs die mid-work on deploy
Is guaranteed by @Async itself
Is handled by the JVM finalizer
quiz.explanation: Production deploys drop unbounded fire-and-forget work unless the pool is a bean with shutdown policy.

quiz.question: Using the common ForkJoinPool for @Async blocking JDBC:
options: Is ideal because FJP is infinite
Starves parallel streams and other FJP users; blocking work needs a dedicated bounded pool
Automatically upgrades to platform threads with no limit
Shares Tomcat's pool
quiz.explanation: Never put blocking IO on the common pool. @Async JDBC belongs on its own executor sized to the DB pool.

quiz.question: @Async method called from a loop of 10k items without batching:
options: Runs sequentially
Enqueues 10k tasks; with a small pool this is a latency/queue-depth bomb, with an unbounded pool an OOM
Spring coalesces the calls
The loop becomes one task
quiz.explanation: Bulk async still needs chunking and a bound. Annotation is not a job queue product.

quiz.question: Which is a valid reason to have more than one @Async executor?
options: Style
Isolate latency-sensitive fan-out from bulk/email/report work so a report storm cannot steal the fan-out threads
Spring requires one executor per method name length
Transactions need their own executor to commit
quiz.explanation: Mixed workloads on one pool create noisy-neighbor outages. Name the pools in @Async("reportsExecutor").

quiz.question: Core size 2, max 16, unbounded queue on the @Async executor. Observed threads stay at 2. Why?
options: Spring caps async at 2
ThreadPoolExecutor only starts extra threads when the queue is full; unbounded queue never fills
max pool is ignored for CPU reasons only
@Async uses core and max as aliases
quiz.explanation: Same Java pool trap, now behind @EnableAsync. Use a bounded queue or a scaling policy that actually fires.

quiz.question: The HTTP request returns 200 because @Async offloaded work, but the user never sees the side effect. First checks?
options: DNS only
Self-invocation, swallowed void exceptions, transaction not committed yet, rejected/queue overflow, executor saturated, lost MDC hiding the error logs
Whether Optional was used
GC promotion only
quiz.explanation: Fire-and-forget has many silent failure modes. Make completion observable.

flashcards.back: Often SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor: new thread per task, no bound. Production code declares a named, bounded ThreadPoolTaskExecutor.
Proxy-based; this.asyncMethod() runs synchronously on the caller thread. Put async methods on another bean.
SecurityContext, MDC, and tenant ThreadLocals do not hop threads. Use a TaskDecorator (and restore/clear in finally).
