Do not reach the caller. AsyncUncaughtExceptionHandler or a Future you actually observe. Otherwise jobs vanish.
The async body does not run in the caller's transaction. Submit after commit if the worker must see persisted rows.
Make the executor a Spring bean with a wait/timeout on destroy, or deploys kill in-flight async work.
JDBC/HTTP inside @Async needs a dedicated pool sized to the dependency, not ForkJoinPool.commonPool().
@Async("name") plus multiple executors isolate bulk work from latency-sensitive fan-out. One shared pool is a noisy neighbor.

quiz.question: In a typical Spring Boot externalized config setup, which source wins over application.properties inside the jar?
options: The jar always wins
Command-line arguments and environment variables override packaged application.properties
Only @PropertySource wins
Random UUID properties
quiz.explanation: Packaged files are defaults. Environment-specific overlay (env vars, CLI, external config files) is meant to win. Never bake secrets as the highest source.

quiz.question: A property appears in both application.properties and application-prod.properties with prod profile active. Which is used?
options: application.properties always
The profile-specific document overrides the same key from the default document
They merge as a list
Spring fails startup on duplicate keys
quiz.explanation: Profile-specific application-{profile} files override the non-profile file for overlapping keys. Later/higher-precedence profiles win among profiles too.

quiz.question: Why does an env var SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL override spring.datasource.url?
options: It does not; names must match exactly including dots
Relaxed binding maps environment variables (and some case/separator variants) onto the dotted property
Only underscores in application.properties work
The DataSource ignores properties
quiz.explanation: Ops can set env vars without dotted keys. The trap is thinking the property is unset because you grepped for the dotted form only.

quiz.question: You set a value in @TestPropertySource and also in application-test.yml. Typical test precedence is:
options: YAML always wins over TestPropertySource
@TestPropertySource / @DynamicPropertySource / @SpringBootTest properties generally override application-test.yml so tests can pin values
The jar's application.properties wins in tests
Profiles are ignored in tests
quiz.explanation: If a test still sees 'wrong' config, a higher source (system property, env, inlined properties) is overlaying it. Dump the environment.

quiz.question: Duplicate keys in the same YAML file across maps vs a dotted key in properties:
options: YAML and properties never collide
The higher-precedence PropertySource wins the flattened key; within one file, last/merge rules can surprise you — treat keys as a single namespace
Nested YAML cannot override dotted keys
Spring keeps both and randomly selects
quiz.explanation: spring.datasource.url and a YAML spring.datasource.url: are the same key after binding. Debugging requires the flattened view.

quiz.question: Config data imported from optional:file:./config/ vs classpath application.properties:
options: Classpath always beats files next to the process
External config locations are intended to override packaged defaults so the same artifact can run in every environment
Files are ignored unless named settings.ini
Import order is random per boot
quiz.explanation: That is the 12-factor overlay. If a local config file is accidentally present in a container, it will silently override what you think is in the image.

quiz.question: @Value("${foo}") vs @ConfigurationProperties for a prefix:
options: They always see different sources

Both read the same Environment, but @Value does not validate unknown keys and binds a single expression; @ConfigurationProperties binds a structured object with conversion and (with the processor) unknown-field policy
@Value ignores env vars
@ConfigurationProperties cannot use relaxed names
quiz.explanation: Production services should prefer @ConfigurationProperties for groups of settings. @Value is easy to miss in the overlay story and has no metadata list.

quiz.question: A command-line --spring.profiles.active=prod vs SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=dev in the environment: what matters?
options: Profiles cannot be set twice
Higher-precedence property source for spring.profiles.active wins; CLI typically beats env, which beats packaged files — know your runtime's actual Environment order
The first profile file on disk wins regardless
Both apply as a random shuffle
quiz.explanation: Conflicting profile activation is a frequent 'wrong config in prod' cause. Log the accepted profiles at startup.

quiz.question: Default values in @Value("${foo:bar}") hide misconfiguration because:
options: Defaults are illegal
If foo is missing from every source, you silently run with bar instead of failing startup
The default always overrides env vars
@Value cannot have defaults
quiz.explanation: For required prod settings (brokers, URLs), fail fast with missing-key errors rather than a default that points at localhost.

quiz.question: spring.application.json / SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON is dangerous in ops because:
options: It cannot set properties
It injects a high-precedence JSON blob of properties that is easy to forget when debugging files and env vars
It only works for logging
It disables relaxed binding
quiz.explanation: When a value 'cannot be found' in files, check this blob and system properties.

quiz.question: Two jars on the classpath both contain application.properties:
options: Spring merges with a documented deterministic library order you should not rely on for overrides; do not ship conflicting keys in libraries
The JVM picks at random each request
Both are illegal and fail startup always
Only the Boot jar's file is read, libraries are ignored always
quiz.explanation: Starter/library application.properties collisions are a classic 'works on my machine' bug. Libraries should use their own prefixes and not a root application.properties if avoidable.

quiz.question: Encrypted values / placeholders that resolve against a later PropertySource fail when:
options: Placeholders always resolve globally after all sources load in one pass with no order issues
A source tries to resolve ${other} before 'other' is present in a higher-precedence source, or circular placeholders exist
Environment variables cannot contain placeholders
@Value does not resolve placeholders
quiz.explanation: Placeholder resolution is order-sensitive. Dump the property origin when a value looks half-substituted.

quiz.question: You change application.yml but Kubernetes still runs old URLs. Most likely:
options: YAML is ignored in containers
A ConfigMap/env/command-line source of higher precedence still has the old key
Relaxed binding is disabled in prod
The bean is prototype so it never rebinds
quiz.explanation: Always inspect the origin of a bound property (actuator env, startup log). File edits do not win if ops overlays them.

quiz.question: The practical way to debug 'which value won?' is:
options: Guess from file timestamps
Inspect the Environment / configprops (with security care): property origin, active profiles, and the bound @ConfigurationProperties object
Recompile until it matches
Print System.getProperties only
quiz.explanation: Origins exist so you do not argue about precedence tables from memory. Lock down actuator exposure when you use them.

flashcards.back: application.properties in the jar are defaults. Env vars, CLI args, and external config locations override them so one artifact can run everywhere.
application-{profile} overrides the same keys in application.properties when that profile is active. Conflicting spring.profiles.active sources are a prod incident waiting.
SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL, spring.datasource.url, and spring.datasource.url in YAML are one property. Grep all forms when debugging.
${foo:localhost} silently ships localhost if foo is unset. Required prod keys should fail startup, not default.
Same Environment, but typed groups, conversion, and metadata. Prefer it for operational config; @Value is a one-off expression.
Command line, SPRING_APPLICATION_JSON, system properties, test inlined properties, and accidental local config files beat what is in the image.
Extra application.properties on the classpath collide. Libraries should not override app keys from a generic file.
Read the Environment/configprops origin for the key and the bound object. Do not argue from a memorized precedence list while three overlays exist.

quiz.question: Leaving /actuator/env and /actuator/configprops fully public is dangerous because:
options: They only show bean names
They can reveal property values, including secrets that landed in the Environment, and which source they came from
They execute arbitrary SQL
They disable authentication globally
quiz.explanation: Env/configprops are a secret dump if keys are not sanitized and the endpoint is unauthenticated or reachable from the internet.

quiz.question: The heapdump and threaddump endpoints are a problem when exposed because:
options: They are read-only and harmless
Heap dumps contain secrets in memory; thread dumps reveal code paths, locks, and sometimes user data in stack frames
They only work locally
They restart the JVM always
quiz.explanation: Treat dump endpoints as equivalent to handing an attacker a memory snapshot. Admin-only, network-isolated.

quiz.question: shutdown and restart actuator operations, if enabled and unauthenticated:
options: Are no-ops
Are remote denial-of-service / control of the process
Only work with a debugger
Require physical access
quiz.explanation: Write endpoints must be off by default in production or gated by strong authz on a private port.

quiz.question: A safe production exposure baseline is:
options: include=*
Expose a minimal health (and maybe info) on the public port; put the rest on a management port locked down by network policy and auth
Expose everything but hide the links in 404 body
Disable health so attackers cannot see it
quiz.explanation: Health is for probes. Everything else is for operators on a private channel. include=* is an incident.

quiz.question: Show-details on health in production without auth:
options: Only adds a boolean
Can leak dependency hostnames, versions, disk paths, and downstream failure details useful to attackers
Is required for Kubernetes probes
Disables the liveness probe
quiz.explanation: Probes need UP/DOWN. Details belong on the management port for humans, not the public health path.

quiz.question: Why a separate management port helps:
options: It makes actuator faster
You can bind it to localhost or a private interface and never publish it on the load balancer that serves the API
It disables all security
It shares the servlet thread pool only
quiz.explanation: Network isolation is stronger than hoping a path prefix is unpublished. Still authenticate.

quiz.question: mappings / beans / conditions endpoints leak:
options: Nothing beyond health
Route tables, internal bean graphs, and auto-config decisions that map the attack surface
Only CSS
User passwords hashed
quiz.explanation: Reconnaissance gold. Keep them off the public internet.

quiz.question: Sanitizing keys in env is insufficient alone because:
options: Sanitization is illegal
Secrets still appear in heapdumps, logs, custom endpoints, and misspelled key names that skip the sanitizer patterns
Env never contained secrets if sanitized
Kubernetes secrets cannot enter the Environment
quiz.explanation: Defense in depth: do not expose env, sanitize anyway, do not print secrets, do not put dumps on the web.

quiz.question: liveness vs readiness on the same unguarded health group:
options: Is ideal
A downstream outage can fail liveness and Kubernetes will kill/restart pods that were only unready, worsening an incident
Kubernetes ignores actuator
Readiness cannot include DB checks
quiz.explanation: Liveness should be 'process is deadlocked/broken'. Readiness can include DB. Splitting them is an actuator design job, not just security.

quiz.question: gateway / proxy that strips /actuator from public routes but forwards /*:
options: Is enough if the string 'actuator' is banned in docs
Can still expose actuators via alternate context paths, management base-path changes, or port mix-ups — verify the actual listener
Makes include=* safe
Disables JMX too
quiz.explanation: Security is on the process bind address and Spring security, not a reverse-proxy string filter you once configured.

quiz.question: JMX exposure of the same actuator operations:
options: Is unrelated
Can bypass HTTP path lockdown if JMX is reachable; lock both HTTP and JMX
JMX cannot invoke shutdown
JMX is always local-only on every OS
quiz.explanation: Two doors, one house. Disable remote JMX unless you treat it as a privileged admin channel.

quiz.question: Logging the full /actuator/health body at INFO on every probe:
options: Is cheap and safe
Can flood logs and record internal dependency errors (and with details on, internals) on a public interval
Is required for metrics
Disables scraping
quiz.explanation: Probes are chatty. Do not log them at info with payloads. Use metrics for probe failure counts.

quiz.question: Custom actuator endpoint that runs a heap query or SpEL from a request parameter:
options: Is fine if unnamed
Is a remote code/data exfil channel; treat custom endpoints with the same authz as admin RCE
Is automatically sanitized
Cannot be mapped under /actuator
quiz.explanation: Actuator is not a safe namespace. Your @Endpoint is production-privileged by default in the operator's mind — attackers agree.

quiz.question: When adding Spring Security, a common misconfig is:
options: Securing /actuator/** and leaving the management port open without security because 'it is private'
Forgetting that permitAll() on /actuator/health also opened sibling endpoints, or that the management port has a separate security filter chain
Actuator ignoring Spring Security always
Health cannot be permitAll even on purpose
quiz.explanation: Two ports, two chains, ant matchers that are too broad. Test unauthenticated GETs against every enabled id, not just health.

flashcards.back: They dump the Environment, including secrets and origins. Public exposure is a credential leak. Sanitize is not a substitute for not exposing them.
Memory and stack snapshots. Secrets, tokens, PII, lock graphs. Admin-only on a private port.
Enables the full attack surface (shutdown, mappings, dumps, env). Production should whitelist the few ids probes need.
Bind actuators to a separate port that is not on the public load balancer. Still authenticate. Network policy is the real gate.
Probes want a boolean. Details leak topology. Keep show-details for authenticated operators, not the internet.
Do not kill pods because a dependency is down. Split groups so liveness is process health and readiness is dependency health.
HTTP lockdown does not close JMX. Remote JMX is another admin API for the same operations.
Unauthenticated GET/POST every enabled endpoint id on both ports. Broad matcher permitAll on /actuator/health is a classic sibling leak.
